lessons.title: The keyboard map
lessons.hook: Every jam this year starts with finding a root note fast, so the map comes first.
lessons.idea: The keys repeat every 12 notes: 7 white, 5 black. The black keys come in groups of two and three, and those groups are your landmarks. C is the white key just left of every group of two; F is just left of every group of three. Middle C is the C nearest the centre of the keyboard (on most pianos, under the brand name). From any C, the white keys spell C D E F G A B and then C again, one octave up. Name a key by its letter and octave: middle C is C4, the C below is C3.

lessons.title: The 12-bar blues
lessons.hook: The blues is the jam you will play first, and its form carries through the whole course.
lessons.idea: A 12-bar blues is a loop of 12 bars, each of four beats, built on three chords named by Roman numerals: I (the home chord), IV (four steps up) and V (five steps up). In C, those are C, F and G. The basic form is: four bars of I, two of IV, two of I, then V, IV, I, V. The last V turns the loop around to start again. Your left hand plays just the root of each chord, once per bar, while counting four. The band plays the same form, so if you get lost, listen for the bass returning to C.

lessons.title: Five notes that always fit
lessons.hook: You can improvise in week one because five notes fit every bar of a blues in C.
lessons.idea: C, D, E, G and A (the C major pentatonic scale) have no notes that clash hard with C7, F7 or G7. Improvising starts with rhythm, not notes: play a short phrase of two to four notes, then rest while the band answers. Repeat a good phrase; change only one note. Land on C or E at the start of a bar when you want the phrase to sound finished. You will be told what you did (how much space, how many chord tones), never that a note was wrong.

lessons.title: Listening guide: a slow blues
lessons.hook: Hearing the form in a real recording makes counting the 12 bars automatic.
lessons.idea: Pick any slow 12-bar blues recording on your streaming service (a classic choice is any version of “St. Louis Blues”, published 1914). Count bars out loud from the first chord. Notice that the singer or soloist plays a phrase, then the band fills the gap: that call-and-response is exactly what your jam does. When you hear the chord change in bar 5, say “four”; in bar 9, say “five”.
lessons.tryIt: Listen to one chorus counting bars. Then play your left-hand roots along with the recording.

check.q: In bar 5 of a blues, which chord arrives?

listening.recording: Any 12-bar blues recording (e.g. “St. Louis Blues”, W. C. Handy, 1914)
listening.listenFor: The change to IV in bar 5 and the call-and-response between voice and band
listening.question: How many bars before the form starts over?

lessons.title: Intervals: steps, skips and leaps
lessons.hook: Reading by interval is faster than naming every note, and it is how you will hear melodies.
lessons.idea: An interval is the distance between two notes. Count letters, including both ends: C to D is a 2nd (a step), C to E a 3rd (a skip), C to G a 5th. On the staff a 2nd moves line to space, a 3rd line to line or space to space, a 5th skips two lines. By ear, a 3rd is the opening of “When the Saints”, a 5th the leap in “Twinkle Twinkle”. Read from a landmark (middle C, treble G, bass F), then read every next note as up or down by an interval.

lessons.title: The scale and the thumb
lessons.hook: The C major scale is the fingering pattern behind every other major scale you will learn.
lessons.idea: Right hand going up: fingers 1 2 3 on C D E, then the thumb passes under to F, then 1 2 3 4 5 on F G A B C. Coming down, finger 3 crosses over the thumb onto E. Left hand going up is the mirror: 5 4 3 2 1 on C D E F G, then finger 3 crosses over to A. Keep the wrist level and let the thumb travel early, under the palm, so the hand moves sideways without a bump.
lessons.tryIt: Play the C scale with the right hand at 60 bpm, two notes per click. Listen for an even sound at the thumb crossing.

check.q: In the right-hand C scale going up, which note does the thumb cross under to?

lessons.title: How to practise a hard spot
lessons.hook: The best pianists in Duke, Simmons and Cash’s 2009 study found the error, fixed it slowly and repeated it clean.
lessons.idea: When a spot fails twice, the app loops just those one or two beats at 70% tempo. Three clean repetitions in a row widen the loop to the bar, then the phrase; then the tempo climbs 4 bpm at a time. Two rules make it work: stop the moment a mistake happens (do not practise the mistake), and keep the loop slow enough that you can play it clean three times running. It feels slower than playing through. It is faster.
lessons.tryIt: Pick one bar of the Saints that you stumble on. Loop it at a tempo where three clean reps are easy.

check.q: How many clean reps in a row widen the loop?

lessons.title: Triads: major and minor
lessons.hook: The Saints in F needs left-hand triads, and every jazz chord grows out of a triad.
lessons.idea: A triad stacks two 3rds: root, 3rd and 5th. A major triad has a major 3rd (4 half steps) on the bottom; a minor triad lowers that 3rd by one key (3 half steps). C major is C–E–G, C minor is C–E♭–G. The symbol tells you which: “F” is F major, “Fm” is F minor. An inversion keeps the same notes with a different note on the bottom; C–E–G, E–G–C and G–C–E are all C major. In the left hand, inversions let you move between chords with tiny steps.

lessons.title: Keys and the circle of fifths
lessons.hook: Jazz tunes live in flat keys, and the circle of fifths is the map of how chords move.
lessons.idea: A key signature lists the sharps or flats a piece uses. G major has one sharp (F♯); F major has one flat (B♭). Going clockwise around the circle of fifths (C, G, D…) adds a sharp each step; anticlockwise (C, F, B♭, E♭…) adds a flat. The anticlockwise direction is also the direction most chord progressions move: from G7 to C, from C7 to F. That is why this course adds keys in the jazz order: C, F, B♭, E♭, then G and A♭.
lessons.tryIt: Play the F major scale and say “B-flat” out loud when you reach it. Then the G major scale, saying “F-sharp”.

lessons.title: Swing eighths
lessons.hook: Swing is the feel that makes the blues sound like jazz rather than a march.
lessons.idea: In swing, a pair of eighth notes is played long–short, roughly like a triplet with the first two notes tied: “doo-ba, doo-ba”. The written notes look even; the feel is not. How long the long note is changes with tempo: slow swing is heavier, fast swing is nearly even. The app measures your long-to-short ratio and tells you how steady it was. It does not mark you wrong for a different ratio — it reports it.
lessons.tryIt: Play C–E–G–E in eighth notes over the band at 80 bpm, swinging. Then check the swing ratio the app reports.

check.q: Is the first or the second eighth note longer in swing?

lessons.title: Five seventh chords
lessons.hook: Seventh chords are the vocabulary of jazz harmony; the blues itself is built from dominant 7ths.
lessons.idea: Add a 7th above a triad and you get a seventh chord. Five qualities cover almost everything: maj7 (major triad + major 7th, C–E–G–B), 7 or dominant 7 (major triad + flat 7th, C–E–G–B♭), m7 (minor triad + flat 7th, C–E♭–G–B♭), m7♭5 or half-diminished (C–E♭–G♭–B♭) and dim7 (C–E♭–G♭–A). The 3rd and 7th decide the quality; the 5th mostly adds weight.

check.q: What makes C7 different from Cmaj7?
check.a: The 7th: B♭ in C7, B in Cmaj7

lessons.title: Shell voicings
lessons.hook: Shells let one hand outline the harmony with two notes, so the other hand is free to solo.
lessons.idea: A shell is the root plus the 7th (or the root plus the 3rd), with the root on the bottom. For the F blues: F7 is F + E♭, B♭7 is B♭ + A♭, C7 is C + B♭. Play them in the left hand between F2 and C4. The app judges shells by the keys you are holding: it names what you are holding as you press, and the chord counts once the right notes have been held together for a moment, so a rolled chord is fine.

lessons.tryIt: Play F7, B♭7 and C7 shells in the blues order with the bass player, one per bar.

check.q: Which two notes make an F7 root–7 shell?

lessons.title: The blues scale
lessons.hook: One six-note scale fits every bar of the blues — the sound of the first gig.
lessons.idea: The F blues scale is F, A♭, B♭, B (the “blue” note), C, E♭. It is the minor pentatonic with one added note. Over F7, the A♭ rubs against the chord’s A — that rub is the blues. Use B as a passing note between B♭ and C, not a note to rest on. Start phrases on F or C, end them on F, and leave as much space as you play.

lessons.tryIt: Play the F blues scale up and down, then make a 4-note phrase from it and repeat it for four bars.

check.q: Which note is added to the minor pentatonic to make the blues scale?

lessons.title: Diatonic sevenths and Roman numerals
lessons.hook: Roman numerals let you learn a progression once and play it in every key.
lessons.idea: Build a seventh chord on every note of the C major scale using only notes from the scale: Cmaj7 (I), Dm7 (ii), Em7 (iii), Fmaj7 (IV), G7 (V), Am7 (vi), Bm7♭5 (vii). Upper case means major, lower case minor. In every major key the pattern of qualities is the same: maj7, m7, m7, maj7, 7, m7, m7♭5.
lessons.tryIt: Play the seven diatonic sevenths in C, root position, saying the numeral for each.

check.q: Which chord is V7 in F major?

lessons.title: The ii–V–I
lessons.hook: Most jazz standards are strings of ii–V–Is; recognising them is how you read a lead sheet quickly.
lessons.idea: ii–V–I is the most common progression in jazz: in C, Dm7–G7–Cmaj7. The roots move up a 4th each time (D to G to C). Better still, the 7th of each chord falls by a half step to become the 3rd of the next: C (7th of Dm7) to B (3rd of G7); F (7th of G7) to E (3rd of Cmaj7). Alternate shells — root–7 on Dm7, root–3 on G7, root–7 on Cmaj7 — and your hand barely moves.
lessons.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 324 72" role="img" aria-label="ii–V–I in C"><rect x="2" y="2" width="80" height="44" fill="#fff" stroke="#000" stroke-width="2"/><text x="42" y="30" font-size="18" font-family="sans-serif" font-weight="700" text-anchor="middle">Dm7</text><rect x="82" y="2" width="80" height="44" fill="#fff" stroke="#000" stroke-width="2"/><text x="122" y="30" font-size="18" font-family="sans-serif" font-weight="700" text-anchor="middle">G7</text><rect x="162" y="2" width="80" height="44" fill="#fff" stroke="#000" stroke-width="2"/><text x="202" y="30" font-size="18" font-family="sans-serif" font-weight="700" text-anchor="middle">Cmaj7</text><rect x="242" y="2" width="80" height="44" fill="#fff" stroke="#000" stroke-width="2"/><text x="282" y="30" font-size="18" font-family="sans-serif" font-weight="700" text-anchor="middle">Cmaj7</text><text x="160" y="66" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">ii–V–I in C</text></svg>
lessons.tryIt: Play the ii–V–I shells in C, then in F (Gm7 C7 Fmaj7), then in B♭ (Cm7 F7 B♭maj7).

check.q: In a ii–V–I in B♭, what is the ii chord?

lessons.title: Reading a lead sheet
lessons.hook: A lead sheet is how jazz musicians share tunes: one line of melody and chord symbols above it.
lessons.idea: A lead sheet gives you the melody on a treble staff and the chord symbols above it. Nobody writes the left hand: you choose the voicing. Read the form first (how many bars, where the repeats are), then the chords for the whole tune, then the melody. Play the left hand on the beat where each symbol appears. If two symbols share a bar, each usually gets two beats.
lessons.tryIt: Open “Two-Five Walk”, read the chord symbols aloud from start to end, then play only the left-hand shells.

check.q: On a lead sheet, who decides the left-hand voicing?

lessons.title: Comping: the Charleston rhythm
lessons.hook: Comping (accompanying) is what a jazz pianist does most of the time.
lessons.idea: The Charleston rhythm plays a chord on beat 1 and again on the “and” of 2, then lets the bar breathe. It is the most common comping rhythm in swing. Two others to know: chords on 2 and 4 (like the hi-hat), and a single anticipation on the “and” of 4 that pushes into the next bar. Keep the chords short and light — comping supports the melody rather than covering it.
lessons.tryIt: Over the Rose Changes vamp, play Gm7 and C7 shells with the Charleston rhythm for 8 bars.

check.q: On which beats does the Charleston rhythm fall?

lessons.title: The 20-hour checkpoint
lessons.hook: After about 66 sessions you should be able to do something a year-one student would be proud of.
lessons.idea: Josh Kaufman’s rule of thumb is that about 20 hours of focused practice gets you past the frustrating start of any skill. This checkpoint asks for two things: a 12-bar blues in F with left-hand shells and two improvised choruses, and the A section of a tune from a lead sheet. Record both as Gig 2. Then compare with your Gig 1 take in the Set List: that comparison is the real reward.
lessons.tryIt: Record the F blues and Rose Changes in one sitting. Listen back once, then write one “fix tomorrow” note.

check.q: Roughly how many 20-minute sessions make 20 hours?

lessons.title: Listening guide: a 1920s ii–V tune
lessons.hook: Hearing how 1920s pianists comped a ii–V vamp makes the Charleston rhythm natural.
lessons.idea: Find a recording of “Honeysuckle Rose” (Fats Waller and Andy Razaf, 1929) on your streaming service. Its A section is the ii–V you have been practising (Gm7–C7 in F). Listen for where the pianist plays chords: often on 1 and the “and” of 2. Count the form: A A B A, eight bars each.
lessons.tryIt: Play your Rose Changes shells along with the recording’s A sections.

check.q: How many bars are in each section of an A A B A tune like this?

listening.recording: “Honeysuckle Rose” (Waller/Razaf, 1929) — any classic recording on a streaming service
listening.listenFor: The Gm7–C7 vamp in each A section and the Charleston comping
listening.question: Where does the bridge (B section) start?
